title: The Late Undertow
premise: Jonah Oyelaran, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost his sense of taste after a childhood fever, has built a career on evocative words that describe nothing he can feel. When Adaeze, the last fluent speaker of Ọ̀rọ̀ Ilẹ̀, a dying Nigerian language, asks him to become her final student, he resists—until he learns she knew his mother and holds photographs that contradict everything Jonah remembers about his family. As his lessons deepen, Jonah must confront the truth that his father's disappearance was not abandonment but exile, and that his own silence has been a form of complicity. In the end, with Adaeze dying, Jonah speaks her language aloud at her funeral—not fluently, but honestly—and finally tastes something again: salt, grief, and the beginning of forgiveness.
about_author: S. M. Winterbourne is the pen name of a former food writer who spent a decade covering West African diaspora cuisine before turning to fiction. They live between Lagos and Lisbon, where they collect recordings of endangered languages.

chapters.title: The Critic Who Cannot Taste
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. We meet him mid-review, writing rapturously about a meal he cannot taste, performing pleasure for readers who trust him. At home he eats plain rice alone. The emotional beat is quiet shame—the gap between his public voice and private emptiness.

chapters.title: A Letter in an Unreadable Hand
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A letter arrives from Adaeze requesting him as her last student, addressed to 'the son of Bisi.' Jonah doesn't know how she knows him. He almost throws it away; instead he pockets it. Beat: curiosity cracking through routine numbness.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, flashback structure. We learn how he lost taste at nine, how his mother Bisi refused to speak their ancestral language afterward, and how Jonah learned to write around absence. Beat: understanding that his whole career is avoidance made elegant.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Remembers Everything
chapters.summary: Jonah visits Adaeze's cramped flat above a shuttered bakery. She is sharp, funny, unimpressed by his byline. She refuses to teach him until he explains why he wants to learn. He can't. Beat: being seen for the first time in years.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Adaeze begins anyway, teaching him greetings. The language has no word for 'critic' but twelve for kinds of listening. Jonah finds himself practicing in the car, embarrassing himself. Beat: tentative joy, the first thing he's wanted in years.

chapters.title: The Photographs
chapters.summary: Adaeze shows him photos from 1980s Lagos: his mother laughing with strangers, his father standing apart, watchful. Jonah realizes the man in the pictures looks afraid, not cold. His childhood memory of a careless father wobbles. Beat: vertigo of unreliable memory.

chapters.title: What Bisi Buried
chapters.summary: Jonah calls his estranged sister Funmi in Manchester; she shuts him down—'Mama said leave it.' He digs through his own storage boxes and finds a hidden cassette labeled in Ọ̀rọ̀ Ilẹ̀ script. Beat: dread mixed with compulsion.

chapters.title: The Review That Fails
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV at work. Mid-lesson, his writing goes hollow—he can no longer perform taste he doesn't have. His editor notices; a rival critic sniffs fraud. Professional identity cracks. Beat: the cost of honesty arriving before the reward.

chapters.title: Adaeze's War
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Her history: a language suppressed by colonial schools, a husband lost, students who quit when it got hard. She chose Jonah deliberately—Bisi once promised her son would carry the words. Beat: we see Jonah as someone else's hope, heavy with obligation.

chapters.title: The Cassette
chapters.summary: Jonah brings the tape to Adaeze. It's his father's voice, recorded the night before he vanished—speaking Ọ̀rọ̀ Ilẹ̀, saying goodbye to baby Jonah in words Jonah now understands for the first time. Beat: devastating reversal; the 'abandonment' was a farewell he couldn't hear.

chapters.title: Funmi's Version
chapters.summary: Jonah travels to Manchester. Funmi reveals what Bisi never said: their father was threatened for documenting the language during a political crackdown, and leaving was protection, not desertion—and Bisi chose silence to keep them safe. Beat: anger redirected from the dead to the living, then softening.

chapters.title: Loyalty Is a Kind of Lie
chapters.summary: Jonah confronts Adaeze: why did she wait thirty years? She admits she promised Bisi she'd never tell—but Bisi's death freed her, and she chose him because he was already half-gone, a man practicing invisibility. Beat: betrayal and gratitude tangled together.

chapters.title: Salt
chapters.summary: After the confrontation, Jonah eats his mother's jollof recipe, cooked badly from memory—and tastes salt. Not flavor exactly, but sensation, grief made physical. Something in him unseals. Beat: fragile breakthrough, earned through pain.

chapters.title: The Rival
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The rival critic publishes an exposé questioning every review Jonah ever wrote. Colleagues distance themselves; an award nomination is quietly withdrawn. Jonah must decide whether to defend the fiction or confess. Beat: public reckoning with private truth.

chapters.title: Confession, Printed
chapters.summary: Jonah writes and publishes the true story: the lost taste, the borrowed words, the language of his fathers. It costs him his column. Readers respond unexpectedly—with their own confessions of performed lives. Beat: humiliation transmuting into connection.

chapters.title: Adaeze Slows Down
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Her health fails; words slip from her mid-sentence. She accelerates the lessons, recording everything, growing impatient and tender by turns. Jonah moves into the spare room to study full-time. Beat: urgency wrapped in love.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Forgiveness
chapters.summary: Adaeze teaches him the language's hardest structure—a verb form used only for releasing old wrongs. To conjugate it, Jonah must say aloud what he forgives: his father, his mother, himself. He manages two of three. Beat: the self-forgiveness withheld, tension held.

chapters.title: Hospital Light
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Adaeze is hospitalized; doctors speak over her in English she pretends not to need. Jonah becomes her translator even into English, insisting on her dignity. He reads her the draft of a book he's writing about her language. Beat: roles reversed—student becoming keeper.

chapters.title: The Last Full Conversation
chapters.summary: Adaeze, lucid one evening, tells Jonah the rest: his father didn't just flee—he carried the language's archive abroad and died trying to bring it home. The stranger in the photographs was a guardian. Jonah speaks the forgiveness verb completely, for all three. Beat: climax of the inner arc.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Adaeze dies on a Tuesday. Jonah, hollowed out, nearly relapses into silence—skips the funeral planning, drafts nothing. Funmi arrives unannounced and sits with him. Beat: grief as undertow, pulling him toward the old invisibility.

chapters.title: Speaking for the Dead
chapters.summary: At the funeral, no one can deliver the eulogy in Ọ̀rọ̀ Ilẹ̀. Jonah stands, imperfect and terrified, and speaks—greetings, the grammar of forgiveness, her name spoken correctly. Elders correct him gently; he accepts correction publicly. Beat: climax of the outer arc; visibility chosen.

chapters.title: What the Mouth Remembers
chapters.summary: Epilogue, six months later. Jonah teaches a small Saturday class of diaspora kids; his new book about Adaeze is underway; he writes a final review—honest, first-person, about a meal he could actually taste. Last line: he cooks his mother's jollof and it tastes like beginning. Beat: resolution, quiet and open.
